versions: 2.7 ∪ 3.x (through 3.13 syntax: match, PEP 695 type parameters and type aliases, except*, parenthesized with-items)

oracles.tool: tools/py-oracle/check.py under python3 (stdin batch, compile(src, path, 'exec'))
oracles.horizon_note: 3.12 rejects syntax newer than itself: PEP 758 (3.14 parenthesis-free multi-except) appears in one black fixture and is booked as noise here; it becomes a gap the day the oracle is bumped, and the bump gets its own before/after sweep.

oracles.tool: tools/py-oracle/check2.py under python2 (stdin batch, compile(src, path, 'exec'); the script is written in the py2/py3 common subset)
oracles.version: CPython 2.7.18, built from source (Ubuntu 24.04 ships no python2 package)
oracles.role: REQUIRED second leg of the union: every file python3 rejects is re-judged, and a file is valid if either accepts. The driver errors loudly if python2 is missing — a py3-only sweep books every py2-only file as noise, which silently hides the py2 half's gaps. Adding this leg surfaced 4 real gap files the py3-only sweep had mis-filed as noise.
oracles.battery: test/negative-oracle/py3/ (print statement, backticks, 0777, except-comma) verified live: python3 rejects all four, python2 accepts all four. test/negative-oracle/py2/ (f-string, nonlocal, walrus) verified live in the reverse direction. The battery caught its own bad fixture on first run: bare `nonlocal x` with no enclosing binding is a SyntaxError in py3 as well, so the fixture gained the enclosing function it needed.
oracles.bug_found_by_widening: The wider corpus crashed the py2 leg: a file with a NUL byte makes py2's compile() raise TypeError where py3 raises ValueError, and check2.py caught only the latter, so the oracle died instead of returning a verdict. A NUL in the source is a VERDICT (the bytes were read fine, they are just not python), not an oracle failure, so both are now caught. The loud-failure discipline worked exactly as designed — the sweep aborted rather than silently booking every python2 file as noise.

corpus.source: top-1000 PyPI packages by download rank (hugovk top-pypi-packages), sdists only; 951 of 1000 publish one
corpus.blind_to: python2-only code (modern PyPI sdists are effectively py3-only, so the py2 half of the union leans entirely on the corpus tests and batteries); notebooks; scripts without .py extension

sweep.oracle_note: adjudicated by the two-leg union oracle (CPython 3.12.3 + 2.7.18).
sweep.noise_note: noise verified by sampling: deliberately-broken test fixtures (jedi completion corpora, ruff/black invalid-syntax fixtures), templating files, and one PEP 758 (py3.14) black fixture — see oracle horizon_note
sweep.note: widened from the top-300 (46,466 files). Every remaining family is a formatter/parser test fixture or a declared deviation; 20 of the 23 are ruff's and black's own edge-case corpora.

corpus.mutation_falsification: while_statement deleted from _loop: 3,661 gap files (vs 23). star_pattern deleted from the match sequence rule: +4. escape_sequence allowed to consume a brace again: 29. Old and new rules alike can be falsified.
corpus.corpus_composition_note: 4 grammar gaps and 12 version-policy rejections. ruff, ty and ast-serialize each vendor ruff's parser test corpus, so every ruff fixture is counted three times: the 4 gaps are 2 distinct sources and the 12 rejections are 3. Exactly one gap file (dill/source.py) is ordinary library code; everything else here is an adversarial parser fixture.

known_gaps.construct: backslash continuations that change a suite's indentation
known_gaps.note: CPython's rule here is neither 'the indent of the first physical line' nor 'the indent of the token'. Taking it from the first physical line (captured at the backslash) FIXES ruff's backslash_continuation_indentation (3 files) and BREAKS black's backslash_before_indent (6 files); the committed behaviour is the reverse trade. Measured both ways, kept the better one.

known_gaps.construct: TWO OR MORE consecutive comment lines after an inline suite
known_gaps.note: One is tolerated. `repeat1` there HANGS the parser — the scanner emits a zero-width NEWLINE at EOF and an unbounded repeat over a zero-width token never terminates. dill/source.py has four.

deviations.what: py2 chevron print `print >> f, x` takes the expression reading (a tuple whose head is a right-shift) — it is valid py3 syntax too, and the union prefers the py3 reading whenever both parse (print_statement carries prec.dynamic(-1))

keywords that were identifiers in some version (True/False/None in py2, async/await before 3.7) are hard keywords here; `True = 5` (py2-valid) does not parse. Soft-keyword machinery exists for print/exec/match/case/type, which carry real corpus weight; the others measured no corpus incidence

`x = 1; if y: pass` (invalid in every version) is accepted when it ends the file: the zero-width NEWLINE the scanner hands out at EOF satisfies the line wrapper the inline suite already consumed. One negative-corpus candidate removed for it; fix wants a smarter EOF rule
inconsistent partial dedents (`if a:` at 0, body at 8, next line at 4) parse; CPython's tokenizer raises IndentationError. The scanner dedents to the nearest enclosing level

escape_sequence never consumes a brace. CPython reads `f"\{foo}"` as a literal backslash followed by an interpolation that still opens, so an escape that swallowed the `{` lost the interpolation entirely; a lone backslash is its own (shorter) alternative, which tree-sitter's longest-match rule keeps out of the way of `\n` and friends.
a format specifier may contain newlines. PEP 701 makes the whole interpolation multi-line inside a triple-quoted f-string, so the closing brace ends the spec rather than the line ending.

deviations.construct: a BLANK line between an inline suite and its continuation clause, e.g. `if True: pass` / `` / `else:`
deviations.was: the scanner emitted NEWLINE for the blank line. `if True: pass` opens no indent level, so the blank line never reached the INDENT/DEDENT branch that consumes such lines -- it fell through to the newline branch, and the spurious NEWLINE committed the shared GLR token stream before `else` could attach.
deviations.now: NEWLINE is emitted only where a line with CONTENT ends: the call started past column 0 and has not already crossed a line boundary. CPython emits NL, not NEWLINE, for blank lines.
deviations.note: Held as LOCAL state in the scan call, not scanner state: tree-sitter persists scanner state only after a call that RETURNS A TOKEN, so a flag cleared on the `return false` path is lost. A first attempt using a persistent flag failed exactly that way. No corpus file exercises it; committed as a correctness fix.

deviations.was: after `f"{num` both `:` and `:=` were valid, and tree-sitter's longest-match rule handed the colon to the walrus: the whole family parsed as `named_expression`. CPython reads it as a width-10 format spec (`'         5'`).
deviations.now: `format_specifier` opens with `token(prec(1, ':'))`. Lexical precedence outranks match length, so this colon wins wherever a format spec can start. It is a distinct token from the plain `:` of dicts, slices and annotations, and a PARENTHESISED walrus -- `f"{(x := 10)}"`, the only form CPython accepts here -- still lexes `:=` because no format spec is valid inside the parentheses.
deviations.note: SILENT except where the spec was not itself a valid walrus right-hand side: only `f"{num:=.2Uf}"` errored, 1 file in mpmath.

deviations.construct: `lambda x: A if c else B`
deviations.was: `(lambda x: A) if c else B` — the conditional wrapped the lambda instead of being its body.
deviations.now: CPython's grammar reads `test: or_test ['if' or_test 'else' test] | lambdef`, so only the ELSE branch may be a bare lambda. `conditional_expression`'s consequence and condition now use an `_or_test` tier that excludes it.
deviations.note: SILENT. Both readings held identical node multisets — one lambda, one conditional — so neither static nor dynamic precedence had anything to weigh; the fix had to remove the ambiguity.

deviations.was: a SET holding one lambda whose parameter was annotated `x: x` and whose body was `1` — the dict's own colon eaten as an annotation.
deviations.now: lambda parameters carry no annotations, which is what Python says, so this is a dict with a lambda key.
deviations.note: SILENT, and a widening as well: annotated lambda parameters were accepted.

deviations.was: the tuple ran across the line break: `x = int,` / `y = 1, 2` became the single chained assignment `x = (int, y) = (1, 2)`. Two statements silently became one.
deviations.now: `prec.right` on `_comma_expressions` had resolved `expr , .` in favour of shifting, which REMOVED the reduce action, so `_newline` was no longer a valid lookahead there and the scanner was never asked for one. Without it the scanner is consulted; a `prec.dynamic` on the tuple then decides the remaining GLR tie, which the two readings differ in — two tuples versus a tuple and a pattern_list.

deviations.construct: a comment between a block and the next statement
deviations.was: the block above owned it, so `if_statement` and `function_definition` spans ran past the construct to the start of the next one. Asking for a statement's source text returned a comment that is not part of it.
deviations.now: the scanner closes open blocks in front of a comment whose next line of CODE is dedented, skipping comment and blank lines for that decision the way CPython's tokenizer does. Not before a continuation clause: `elif`/`else`/`except`/`finally` mean the statement is not over, and closing early kills the fork waiting for the clause.
deviations.note: Matters most to anything that re-emits code.

roles_note: 18 of 22 table-tier terms are threaded. Omitted: _type (python annotations are ordinary expressions — the vocabulary's own position), _modifier (python has no named modifier nodes yet; async/await are anonymous), _control_flow (unthreadable here: a supertype's members enter every position that references it, and clauses/jump-vs-branch positions are construct-specific — see the uncategorised reasons in roles.json). _clause MOVED to the facet tier in vocabulary 0.2.0 on exactly this evidence, gathered independently in python, rust and typescript; _control_flow remains the open candidate.
patterns_note: match patterns are a dedicated sub-grammar (PEP 634), not the expression rules. The shapes reuse the destructuring node names by alias — `(tuple_pattern)`, `(list_pattern)`, `(star_pattern)` mean the same thing in `a, b = x` and in `case (a, b)` — but they are NOT threaded through the `_pattern` supertype, and that is a measured decision rather than an oversight: python's destructuring and match positions admit different member sets (`x[0]` and `*rest` destructure but do not match; `Point(x=0)` and `{'k': v}` match but do not destructure), and a supertype's members enter every position that references it. Routing them through `_pattern` made `a, Point(x=0) = z` parse, which CPython rejects. This is the `_clause` law in a second place; rust does not hit it because its `let` and `match` patterns are one set. Consequence: `(_pattern)` covers destructuring positions here, and match patterns are reached by their shared concrete names.
version_policy: DESIGN.md §4.2: where a construct is valid only in an older version AND admitting it would change how current code parses, the current language wins. Three constructs are rejected on purpose — `f((a)=1)` (py3.0–3.7), bare `nonlocal` (py2), bare `await` (py2, py3.0–3.4). Declared with reasoning in version_policy.json, gated by test/negative/, and booked by the sweep as `version` rather than `gap`. Older syntax with no competing reading in any later version stays ACCEPTED (`except E, e:`, py2 print/exec, backticks, old octal) — that is most of what the py2 half of the union is.
shape_check: `treebank shape` compares our node BOUNDARIES against CPython `ast` over the whole corpus: 112,138,339 oracle nodes across 137,876 files, 0 missed. It started at 1,682,942. Everything left is declared in shape_policy.json as a granularity difference with its reasoning — CPython nests `elif` as a new If, starts a FunctionDef at `def` rather than the decorator, splits parameter defaults into a parallel list, folds implicitly concatenated strings, and treats BoolOp as n-ary. 1,329 files are skipped: python2-only sources, and files whose PEP 263 coding declaration or BOM means `ast` reports offsets into a byte string that is not the one on disk.

known_widenings.construct: `f(a=1, b)` — a positional argument after a keyword argument
known_widenings.why_accepted: `arguments` is a flat comma list of `_argument`, so nothing orders the two kinds. CPython rejects it: "positional argument follows keyword argument".
known_widenings.found_by: `treebank mutate` — deleting the `=` from a keyword argument turns it into a positional one, and the grammar was happy either way. The first thing that check found.
known_widenings.why_not_fixed: The fix works and costs a vocabulary guarantee. Ordering needs the two groups to have DIFFERENT element sets, which means two hidden rules; tree-sitter supertypes are derivation-based, so whichever group does not route through `_argument` stops answering `(_argument)`. The vocabulary defines that term as `actual argument position in an invocation`, so silently narrowing it to keyword arguments only is worse than a declared widening. Left as a decision to take deliberately.

known_widenings.why_accepted: `escape_sequence` has a lone-backslash alternative, needed so `f"\{foo}"` keeps its interpolation. With it, `\x` reads as an escaped backslash followed by content. CPython requires exactly two hex digits and errors otherwise.
known_widenings.why_not_fixed: Removing the fallback breaks the f-string case; requiring well-formed \x/\u/\U needs the string scanner to stop differently. Real, and bigger than a rule edit.

known_widenings.construct: a keyword as an attribute name, `a.None` / `a.True`
known_widenings.why_accepted: the attribute position takes `_name`, which reaches the keyword literals.
known_widenings.why_not_fixed: `a.True` is valid python2 (`True` was a builtin, not a keyword), so this is also a version-policy question — under §4.2 the current language wins and it should be rejected. `a.None` is invalid in every version and has no such excuse.

mutation_check: `treebank mutate` — 4,508 mutants over 594 corpus files, 102 widenings in 83 clusters. The sweep measures rejects-valid over 139,205 files; this measures the other direction, which test/negative/ had been measuring with eighteen hand-written ones.
error_positions: `treebank errors` — 926 of 935 rejected files are comparable (both parsers reject): 205 exact, 535 within 16 bytes, 153 within 128, 33 further. Median |delta| 5 bytes. The tail is almost all jedi's completion fixtures, which are deliberately truncated snippets.
lexical_check:
`treebank shape` also compares TOKEN boundaries against CPython's `tokenize`, the only oracle we have below the tree. Zero disagreements once three f-string granularity differences are declared in shape_policy.json. Two bugs were found building it, both in the checker: `tokenize` reports CHARACTER columns where `ast` reports UTF-8 BYTE columns, and `splitlines()` breaks on 
, \x0c and   where the line table counts 
. One bug was found in the grammar: `comment` was `token(seq('#', /.*/))`, and tree-sitter's `.` excludes 
 but MATCHES , so every comment in a CRLF file ended one byte late.
roundtrip_check: `treebank roundtrip` — 139,205 files re-rendered through `ast.unparse` and reparsed: 137,968 rendered (1,237 declined by the printer, mostly python2-only sources), 3 failures. All three are the same ruff fixture vendored three times, and what it exposed is not a round-trip problem at all: `case y if a if True else b:` is a real gap, and the sweep had filed it as NOISE because the validity oracle uses `compile()`, which ALSO rejects the file for `'yield' outside function` -- a semantic check, not a syntactic one. `ast.parse` accepts the file. The oracle is stricter than a parser and has been understating gaps; correcting that is its own change.
